text.p: The president of COR Therapeutics Inc said Tuesday the company hopes to file for approval of a drug for severe heart disease by late 1997 or early 1998, despite a recent setback in the review process.

COR president and CEO Vaughn Kailian spoke to Reuters after receiving a letter from the Food and Drug Administration advising that Phase III trial data on the drug, Integrilin, were insufficient to support approval.
He said COR remains confident that Integrilin helps prevent heart attacks in patients with unstable angina and in those undergoing angioplasty to clear blockages.

COR and its partner Schering-Plough Corp initially applied for approval of Integrilin in April 1996. Phase III trial trial data submitted with its application showed the drug reduced by 20 percent the incidence of heart attacks or other serious "events" following angioplasty, but that rate of improvement was not considered statistically significant.

Kailian said COR will have new data this summer from a second, larger Phase III trial testing Integrilin in patients with unstable angina, a condition that often triggers heart attacks much the same way angioplasty does. He said dosing levels were increased substantially in the second trial.

He added that while there are a lot of potential reasons why Integrilin did not produce more robust trial results, COR has "a reasonable level of confidence that we needed to go up in the dose." However, he said that since the ongoing trial was blinded, he was unable to comment on how it was progressing. "Obviously this is a very large trial and we expect, or we hope to be successful," he said.

In both trials, Integrilin is aimed at blood clots that form and lead to heart attacks. Derived from rattlesnake venom, the drug prevents platelets from accumulating at injury sites in the blood vessels, a common cause of heart attack.

While angioplasty is often seen as a routine procedure, it actually carries a high risk, leading to heart attack, death or the need for urgent reintervention like surgery about eight percent of the time. The rate of heart attack or death in patients with unstable angina is also about eight percent.
Kailian said COR had about $53 million of cash on hand, which it sees as sufficent to sustain it through the delayed approval process.
